chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him), who said:
The one who performs li'an (conjugal imprecation) does so only by denying the child, and he said: When a man accuses his wife [of adultery], he performs li'an with her.

key_terms.قَذَفَ: To accuse or throw [charges of adultery] at someone.
key_terms.لَعان: Li'an (conjugal imprecation), a legal procedure where a husband accuses his wife of adultery and denies paternity, involving sworn oaths.
key_terms.نَفْيِ وَلَدٍ: Denial of the child, the specific condition required for the li'an ritual to take place.

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for li'an to be valid according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies a key jurisprudential nuance in Shia law: the ritual of li'an is contingent upon the husband explicitly denying paternity of the offspring, rather than merely accusing the wife of adultery. It establishes that the legal mechanism for expiating the accusation and confirming lineage is activated specifically when the child's lineage is disputed, aligning with the broader principles of evidence in the Quran. This distinction ensures that li'an serves as a precise legal tool for resolving paternity disputes rather than a general penalty for adultery.
